meta.title: Operations
meta.range: HSC topic · 25% of course time · strategies for effective operations management in large businesses

boxes.label: Examinable
boxes.bodyHtml: Role of operations management, transformation processes (inputs, transformation, outputs), the 4 Vs, operations strategies (performance objectives, supply chain management, technology, quality management, overcoming resistance to change) and global factors — all Learn To and Learn About dot points.

boxes.label: Format reminder
boxes.bodyHtml: The HSC Business Studies exam draws on all four topics: Section I is 20 multiple-choice questions, Section II is short-answer questions spanning all topics, Section III is a business-report extended response, and Section IV offers a choice of extended-response questions by topic.

summary.note: Organised by the syllabus's own headings for this topic.

groups.title: Role of operations management
points: Operations refers to the processes involved in the transformation of inputs (raw materials, labour, facilities, information) into outputs (finished goods and services).

The strategic role of operations management is long-term planning performed by senior managers, achieving maximum output with minimum input (efficiency) to add value — the output should be worth more than the combined inputs.

Effective operations management adds value by increasing productivity, reducing costs and improving quality, achieved through cost leadership (competing on lower prices) and/or good/service differentiation (competing on unique features). Real example: Kmart's own-brand Anko strategy — designing in-house, sourcing directly and standardising ranges — delivered FY2025 Kmart Group earnings of $1,046 million, up 9.2%, on revenue growth of only 2.9%, showing the margin was made in operations, not price.
Operations is a cost centre — it doesn't directly generate income, but generates costs the business must manage.

The range of goods/services a business offers differs by industry: standardised vs customised goods, perishable vs non-perishable goods, and intermediate goods (finished products that become another business's input, e.g. milk sold to bakeries).

Interdependence is the mutual dependence the four key business functions have on each other — e.g. marketing communicates customer needs so operations can plan production; finance provides funds that determine which operations strategies are affordable; HR supplies and trains the staff operations processes need.

groups.title: Influences on operations management
points: Globalisation widens sourcing options and markets but increases competition. Real example: DP World Australia handles about 40% of the nation's container freight, and Kmart's Anko brand — sourced globally — is now sold offshore through stores in the Philippines and wholesale partnerships with major overseas retailers.

Technology can transform operations at scale. Real example: Woolworths opened a $1.3 billion automated National and Regional Distribution Centre at Moorebank in Western Sydney on 18 November 2025 — its largest single investment ever — moving over five million cartons a week to 1,000+ stores and removing an estimated 26,000 truck movements a year. But dependence on technology carries risk: a cyber attack on DP World Australia's port terminals over 10–13 November 2023 stranded around 30,000 containers and halted national freight movement for days.

Quality expectations shape operations decisions on both product and process quality. Real example: Bunnings' Total Recordable Injury Frequency Rate (TRIFR) improved from 17.0 in FY2024 to 13.7 in FY2025 — still the weakest safety result in the Wesfarmers group, showing quality of process (workplace safety) is monitored the same way as quality of output.

Cost-based competition pushes operations toward efficiency gains. Real example: Kmart Group's FY2025 earnings grew 9.2% against revenue growth of only 2.9% — evidence operations strategy, not pricing, drove the margin.

Government policies and legal regulation constrain how operations can be run. Real example: the NSW EPA issued Clean-Up Notices requiring the removal of 4,000 tonnes of stockpiled soft plastics from 15 sites across NSW (completed by mid-2025) after the collapse of the REDcycle recycling scheme; separately, the Privacy Commissioner found in November 2024 that Bunnings' in-store facial recognition technology (used November 2018 – November 2021) breached the Privacy Act, with the Administrative Review Tribunal upholding the transparency and notification findings in February 2026.

Environmental sustainability is increasingly built into operations processes, not treated as an afterthought. Real example: the Moorebank distribution centre is 5-star Green Star rated with 5.3MW of rooftop solar and rainwater harvesting.

Corporate social responsibility (CSR) goes beyond legal compliance to an ethical responsibility toward the 'triple bottom line' — social, environmental and financial impact — even though it isn't required by law. Real example: when REDcycle stopped processing soft plastics in November 2022, Coles and Woolworths were not legally responsible for the collapse of a third-party scheme, but took responsibility for funding the clean-up anyway — the clearest illustration that ethical responsibility runs further than legal compliance.

groups.title: Operations processes
points: Inputs are classified as transformed resources (materials, information, customers — the things converted during production) and transforming resources (human resources and facilities — the things that carry out the conversion).

The 4 Vs shape operations processes based on customer demand: Volume (how much to make — high volume favours standardisation and economies of scale, low volume favours customisation), Variety (how many product variations — higher variety raises costs and needs more flexible technology), Variation in demand (how much demand fluctuates and how quickly operations can respond), and Visibility (how much direct customer contact/input there is, e.g. a hairdresser vs a factory). Real example: Qantas is the standard tertiary-industry example — its product (a seat) is intangible, perishable (an unsold seat is lost forever) and highly customer-contact intensive; Canva, by contrast, produces a digital service with near-zero marginal cost, so its operations challenge is capacity and reliability rather than physical transformation.

Sequencing is the order activities occur in; scheduling is how long each activity takes. Gantt charts give a quick overview of tasks and timing but don't show task relationships; Critical Path Analysis (CPA) shows how tasks are interrelated and identifies the longest (critical) path, but both struggle with very complex projects or inaccurate time estimates.

Technology used in operations includes robotics (precision, consistency, efficiency), CAD (computer-aided design, 3D visualisation) and CAM (computer-aided manufacturing, linking design to production) — businesses choose between leading-edge technology (the newest available, offering a first-mover advantage but at higher cost and risk of early faults) and established technology (proven and cheaper, but offering less of a competitive edge).

Task design — how a job is broken into specific tasks and combined with the process layout — should match the transformation process being used, since poorly designed tasks slow throughput and raise error rates regardless of how good the layout or technology is.

Process layout groups equipment by function (e.g. restaurants); product layout arranges equipment by the sequence of tasks, suited to large-volume standardised production (e.g. assembly lines); fixed position layout brings employees and equipment to the product (e.g. building a house).

Monitoring measures actual performance against planned performance using KPIs (key performance indicators); control takes corrective action when KPIs miss targets; improvement systematically reduces inefficiencies and bottlenecks, often through kaizen (continuous improvement).

Outputs include the goods/services themselves, customer service (meeting or exceeding expectations) and warranties (a legal promise to fix defects) — both are also useful sources of feedback for monitoring operations.

groups.title: Operations strategies
points: Performance objectives (QSDFCC): quality, speed, dependability, flexibility, customisation and cost — targets operations managers aim to meet in order to build a competitive advantage.

New product/service design and development happens either in response to consumer preferences (market research) or from advances in technology, and must balance quality, supply chain, capacity and cost.

Supply chain management covers sourcing (including global sourcing), logistics and e-commerce; a business's supply chain is its supply network and relationship with suppliers. Real example: Kmart's Anko brand is designed in-house and sourced directly from overseas manufacturers, cutting out intermediaries to achieve cost leadership.

Outsourcing (contracting activities to an external business, onshore or offshore) can lower costs and improve process capability, but risks loss of control, communication issues and loss of corporate memory.

Inventory management approaches include FIFO (first-in-first-out, suited to perishables — lowers cost of goods sold and raises gross profit), LIFO (last-in-first-out, suited to non-perishables like fast fashion) and JIT (just-in-time, minimal stock ordered only when needed) which reduces storage costs but requires reliable suppliers and accurate demand forecasts. Real example: the November 2023 cyber attack on DP World Australia stranded around 30,000 containers and halted freight nationally for days in the lead-up to Christmas — a stark illustration of the trade-off inside JIT, since minimal inventory is efficient until a single node in the supply chain fails and there is no buffer stock left to fall back on.

Quality management has three approaches: quality control (reactive — inspecting and fixing defects), quality assurance (proactive — designing processes to prevent defects) and total quality management/continuous improvement (an ongoing, business-wide commitment via benchmarking and employee empowerment).

Overcoming resistance to change involves financial factors (new equipment, redundancy payments, retraining, reorganising plant layout) and psychological factors (inertia — fear of being replaced, fear of the new, preference for stability) — addressed by evaluating change thoroughly, being proactive, implementing gradually, involving employees, and using change agents.

Global factors — global sourcing, economies of scale, scanning and learning (learning from successful practices worldwide, e.g. post-WWII Japanese kaizen), and research and development (R&D) — help businesses compete internationally, though Australia's R&D investment ranks comparatively low among OECD countries.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the strategic role of operations management.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define strategic (long-term planning by senior managers).
  • Explain efficiency (maximum output, minimum input).
  • Link to cost leadership and/or differentiation as the strategic goal.
Sample answer

The strategic role of operations is the long-term planning performed by senior managers, done efficiently by achieving the maximum output with the minimum level of inputs. This means transforming inputs such as raw materials, labour and facilities into outputs as finished goods and services, while increasing productivity, reducing costs and improving quality. This is done to achieve a strategic competitive advantage through cost leadership (competing on lower prices, e.g. Aldi and Chemist Warehouse minimise the cost of production to sell for less) and/or differentiation (competing through special characteristics such as better quality, faster delivery or clever design, e.g. Ferrari and Apple). Operations assists the business in achieving its overall goal of profit maximisation by adding value, so the output is worth more than the combined inputs.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how interdependence between operations and the other key business functions can affect a business.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define interdependence.
  • Give an example linking operations to at least two other functions.
Sample answer

Interdependence is the mutual dependence the four key business functions have on each other to perform efficiently and achieve common goals like profit maximisation. Operations and marketing must communicate to ensure products meet the standards customers expect and are ready by the date marketing promotes them for. Finance provides the funds that determine which operations strategies (like investment in new technology) can be undertaken — this investment can lead to faster processing speeds and less waste, resulting in savings on labour and materials. Human resources must hire and train employees with the right skills to operate machinery, and when operations outsources or automates a process, HR must manage the resulting redundancies. None of the four functions can operate effectively in isolation.

questions.questionHtml: Two Australian gym chains operate in the same suburbs. FitBase charges $15 a week for 24-hour swipe-card access to a single large warehouse-style space with no classes or staff on site. Elevate Studio charges $65 a week for a staffed front desk, a full group-fitness class timetable and personal-training packages. Using the stimulus, distinguish between cost leadership and good/service differentiation as strategic approaches to operations management.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define both approaches.
  • Apply each to the gym in the stimulus that uses it.
  • Note the operations decisions each approach implies.
Sample answer

Cost leadership competes by minimising the cost of production so the business can sell at the lowest price. FitBase is pursuing cost leadership: an unstaffed, single-format space with no classes strips labour and facility costs out of the operations process, letting it charge a fraction of a typical gym membership.

Good/service differentiation competes on special characteristics other than price — quality, convenience or customer experience. Elevate Studio is pursuing differentiation: staffed reception, a full class timetable and personal training all add cost to the operations process, but justify a price more than four times FitBase's by offering a noticeably more supported experience. Both are legitimate operations strategies for building a competitive advantage in the same market — the difference is whether the business competes by minimising inputs or by adding value that customers will pay more for.

questions.questionHtml: Two Australian furniture retailers sell similar-looking sofas online. BaseForm sources one standard design in three colours, ships flat-packed and offers no assembly or design service, priced at $499. Woodhouse Living offers made-to-order upholstery in over 200 fabric options, free in-home design consultations and white-glove delivery, priced at $2,800. Using the stimulus, distinguish between cost leadership and good/service differentiation as strategic approaches to operations management.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define cost leadership and differentiation.
  • Apply cost leadership to BaseForm.
  • Apply differentiation to Woodhouse Living.
Sample answer

Cost leadership is an operations strategy of minimising the cost of inputs and processes so a business can compete on the lowest price, while differentiation is a strategy of adding distinctive features so customers are willing to pay a premium. BaseForm is pursuing cost leadership: a single standard design in flat-pack form removes the cost of custom manufacturing, in-home consultations and white-glove delivery, stripping cost out of the transformation process so it can sell at under $500. Woodhouse Living is pursuing differentiation: made-to-order upholstery, an extensive fabric range and a design and delivery service all add value that competitors don't match, which is what justifies a price more than five times BaseForm's. Both are valid ways to build competitive advantage — the risk for BaseForm is a price war eroding its thin margins, while Woodhouse's risk is that its far higher cost base leaves it exposed if customers become more price-sensitive.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the interdependence between the operations function and TWO other key business functions.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define interdependence.
  • Link operations to marketing.
  • Link operations to human resources or finance.
Sample answer

Interdependence is the mutual reliance the key business functions have on one another to achieve the business's overall objectives. Operations depends on marketing to forecast demand accurately, since producing too much ties up cash in unsold stock and producing too little means lost sales and unhappy customers — and marketing in turn depends on operations to deliver a product that actually matches what was promised in its campaigns, or the business risks refunds and reputational damage. Operations is equally interdependent with human resources: operations needs appropriately skilled, available staff rostered onto the transformation process to hit output and quality targets, while HR relies on operations to specify what skills and how many staff are actually required. A breakdown in either relationship — for example, marketing launching a promotion operations wasn't resourced to fulfil — shows why these functions cannot be managed in isolation from one another.

questions.questionHtml: Using a real example, explain how technology has influenced the operations strategy of a large business.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Name a real business and a specific, dated technology decision.
  • Link the technology to at least one operations outcome (cost, speed, sustainability).
  • Note a trade-off or risk of technology dependence.
Sample answer

Woolworths opened a $1.3 billion automated National and Regional Distribution Centre at Moorebank in Western Sydney on 18 November 2025 — its largest single investment ever, replacing older manual warehouses with automated storage and retrieval. The site can move more than five million cartons a week to over 1,000 stores nationally, and is expected to remove an estimated 26,000 truck movements from Australian roads each year, while being 5-star Green Star rated with 5.3MW of rooftop solar.

This shows technology can lift multiple performance objectives at once — speed, cost and environmental sustainability — by converting a variable labour cost into a fixed capital cost. However, technology dependence also carries risk: the November 2023 cyber attack on DP World Australia's port terminals, which handle around 40% of the nation's container freight, stranded roughly 30,000 containers and halted freight movement nationally for several days. Together these show technology as an influence cuts both ways — it can dramatically improve operations performance, but concentrates risk onto fewer, larger, more critical systems.

questions.questionHtml: Using a real example, distinguish between legal compliance and ethical responsibility in operations management.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define both terms.
  • Use one real, dated example that shows the gap between them.
Sample answer

Legal compliance is meeting the minimum standard required by law; ethical responsibility goes beyond that minimum to what a business believes is the right thing to do, even where it isn't legally required.

When the REDcycle soft plastics recycling scheme stopped processing collected material in November 2022, thousands of tonnes of plastic that Coles and Woolworths customers had dropped off in good faith were found stockpiled rather than recycled. Neither supermarket was legally responsible for the failure of a third-party scheme, but both took responsibility for funding the clean-up under a soft plastics taskforce, working through NSW EPA Clean-Up Notices that ultimately covered removal of 4,000 tonnes of stockpiled plastic from 15 sites. This is one of the clearest available examples of the gap between legal compliance and ethical responsibility in operations: the supermarkets acted because consumers held them responsible for the outcome of a program bearing their name, not because the law required it.

questions.questionHtml: An Australian toy manufacturer has moved 80% of its component sourcing to suppliers in Indonesia and Thailand, and now sells through online marketplaces in fifteen countries. Explain how globalisation has influenced the operations strategy of this business.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define globalisation.
  • Explain the opportunity global sourcing creates.
  • Explain a challenge it creates.
Sample answer

Globalisation is the increasing economic interdependence between countries, seen here in the business's access to overseas suppliers and overseas customers. Sourcing 80% of components from Indonesia and Thailand is a cost-leadership opportunity: overseas manufacturing typically offers significantly lower labour costs than Australia, letting the business reduce its cost of inputs and either lift its margin or compete more aggressively on price. Selling through online marketplaces in fifteen countries also expands its addressable market well beyond what a domestic-only operation could reach, supporting economies of scale in production. However, globalisation also introduces new risks to operations strategy: longer, more complex supply chains are more exposed to shipping delays, exchange rate movements and quality-control problems that are harder to manage at a distance, so the business must now build additional lead time and supplier-monitoring processes into its operations that a purely domestic manufacturer would not need.

questions.questionHtml: A cosmetics manufacturer producing 60 million units a year has committed to using fully recyclable packaging by 2027 and to cutting energy use per unit produced by a quarter. Assess the impact on this business of adopting environmentally sustainable operations practices.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Identify a benefit of the commitment.
  • Identify a cost or challenge.
  • Weigh the two and reach a judgement.
Sample answer

Adopting these sustainability commitments will impose real short-term costs on the business: switching to fully recyclable packaging and redesigning processes to cut energy use per unit by a quarter will require investment in new packaging suppliers and more energy-efficient equipment, and at this scale (60 million units a year) even small per-unit cost increases become significant in total. Against this, the commitments offer meaningful benefits — reduced long-term input costs once recyclable packaging and lower energy use are built into standard operations, a stronger position with increasingly environmentally conscious retailers and consumers, and reduced exposure to future regulation or resource scarcity around packaging materials and energy. On balance, for a business operating at this volume, the reputational and regulatory-risk benefits of getting ahead of sustainability expectations are likely to outweigh the transition costs over the medium term, even though the upfront capital investment will reduce short-term profitability.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how the 4 Vs (volume, variety, variation in demand and visibility) influence a business's transformation processes.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define each of the 4 Vs briefly.
  • Explain the effect of each on production costs/processes, with an example.
Sample answer

Volume refers to how much of a product is made — high-volume businesses like a fast-food chain use standardised inputs and more capital and technology, achieving economies of scale, while low-volume businesses like a fine-dining restaurant use more multi-skilled labour and allow customisation.

Variety refers to how many different models or variations a business offers. Greater variety requires more inputs and more flexible (and often more expensive) technology, as seen in prosthetics manufacturing, which is low-volume but high-variety.

Variation in demand is how much demand fluctuates, and how well a business can respond — an air-conditioning manufacturer faces high seasonal variation, while a cafe has low variation year-round. Poor responsiveness to rising demand causes lost sales; poor responsiveness to falling demand causes overproduction and wastage.

Visibility is the degree of direct customer contact with the operations process. A hairdresser has high visibility, as the customer shapes the output directly, while a business producing standardised office supplies has low visibility. High volume, low variety, low variation and low visibility generally lower production costs through economies of scale and reduced flexibility requirements.

questions.questionHtml: Using a real example, discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using just-in-time (JIT) inventory management.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define JIT.
  • Give an advantage and a disadvantage.
  • Support the disadvantage with a real, dated example.
Sample answer

Just-in-time (JIT) is an inventory control system where inventories are kept at minimum levels and stock is only ordered when required, aiming to hold as little inventory as possible.

Advantages include reduced storage space requirements, easier stocktaking, and cost savings on storage and waste, since the business isn't holding large amounts of unsold inventory that could become obsolete. The key disadvantage is reduced ability to cope with a disruption to supply, since there's little or no buffer stock. This was demonstrated when DP World Australia — which handles around 40% of the nation's container freight — was hit by a cyber attack on 10–13 November 2023, stranding approximately 30,000 containers and halting freight movement nationally for several days, in the lead-up to Christmas. Businesses relying on JIT inventory from those ports had no buffer stock to fall back on, and economists estimated the disruption cost businesses millions of dollars a day.

For JIT to work, a business needs a clear understanding of consumer demand, flexible production, and reliable suppliers who can deliver frequently and in low volumes — without this, a JIT system risks stockouts and lost sales exactly when a single point of failure occurs.

questions.questionHtml: A packaging manufacturer runs two production lines. Line X makes a single box design in batches of 80,000. Line Y makes 210 different custom box designs, with an average batch of 150 and a ninety-minute changeover between designs. Explain how volume and variety influence the transformation processes of this business.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain the effect of high volume on Line X.
  • Explain the effect of high variety on Line Y.
Sample answer

Volume and variety are two of the key factors that shape how a transformation process should be designed. Line X's very high volume and low variety (one box design, 80,000-unit batches) suit a highly standardised, repetitive process — specialised, dedicated equipment and a product layout can be justified because the same task is being repeated at large scale, driving the cost per unit down. Line Y's low volume and very high variety (210 different designs, small 150-unit batches) require the opposite approach: flexible, general-purpose equipment and a process layout that can be reconfigured for each design, even though the ninety-minute changeover between designs reduces the line's overall output and increases the cost per unit. This shows why a single 'best' transformation process doesn't exist — the right design depends entirely on where a specific line sits on the volume–variety spectrum.

questions.questionHtml: Distinguish between a product layout and a process layout.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define product layout and give an example business.
  • Define process layout and give an example business.
  • Note the type of production each suits.
Sample answer

A product layout arranges equipment and workstations in the sequence needed to make one standardised product, as on a car assembly line, where every unit moves through the same fixed sequence of stations — this suits high-volume, low-variety production because it minimises movement and allows specialisation, but it is inflexible and a fault at one station can stop the whole line. A process layout instead groups similar equipment or skills together, as in a hospital where X-ray, pathology and surgical departments are separate areas a patient moves between depending on their needs — this suits low-volume, high-variety operations because it is far more flexible to different requirements, though it typically means more movement and time between stages than a product layout achieves for a single standardised product.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how technology can provide a business with a competitive advantage in its operations.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Link technology to cost leadership and/or differentiation.
  • Support with a named example.
Sample answer

Technology can create a competitive advantage through cost leadership, as processes run more efficiently, safely and without error, lowering production costs — for example, Apple outsources manufacturing to Foxconn, whose robots perform dangerous or repetitive tasks with fewer employees, reducing labour costs. Technology can also create a competitive advantage through differentiation, since less human error improves product quality and enables the development of new products — for example, Amazon uses robots to attach barcodes and track items, making supply chain management more efficient and reliable. Both cost savings and improved quality allow the business to increase revenue, either through lower prices or higher prices justified by better quality.

questions.questionHtml: Compare quality control, quality assurance and total quality management as approaches to quality management.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define each of the three approaches.
  • Note whether each is reactive or proactive.
Sample answer

Quality control is a reactive strategy — employees inspect products at various stages of production, using preset quality standards, to find and correct defects before they reach customers. It only detects faults rather than preventing them.

Quality assurance is a proactive system that establishes procedures and processes — such as designing products to be fit for purpose and complying with international standards — to prevent defects occurring in the first place, saving time, money and energy compared to fixing problems after the fact.

Total quality management (TQM) goes further, aiming to manage the entire business so customers receive consistently high-quality goods and services, relying on continuous improvement across all functional areas (not just operations), benchmarking against competitors, and empowering every employee to suggest improvements. Together these three approaches move from reactive fault-finding, to proactive prevention, to an ongoing business-wide culture of quality.

questions.questionHtml: Discuss how a business could overcome employee resistance to change when introducing new operations technology.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Identify a psychological reason for resistance (inertia).
  • Identify at least one financial factor.
  • Recommend at least two change-management strategies.
Sample answer

Employees often resist change due to inertia — a psychological resistance stemming from fear of being replaced (e.g. by robotics), fear of learning new and unfamiliar skills, or simply a preference for stability. Change also brings financial factors like the cost of new equipment, redundancy payments for employees whose roles are no longer needed, and retraining costs.

To overcome this resistance, a business should evaluate the sources of change thoroughly before acting, to avoid creating even more resistance. Being proactive — anticipating change rather than being forced into it — gives the business more control and avoids rushed decisions. Implementing change gradually gives employees time to adjust, reducing resistance, and including employees in the process by communicating transparently about why the change is necessary builds buy-in. Businesses can also bring in change agents, internal or external, to facilitate the transition and provide practical tools and guidance.

questions.questionHtml: Using a real example, examine the impact of globalisation on operations strategy.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define globalisation.
  • Cover both opportunities and threats.
  • Support with a real, dated example.
Sample answer

Globalisation is the increasing interconnectedness and interdependence of people and businesses worldwide, widening the potential market and creating both opportunities and threats for operations strategy.

Global sourcing lets businesses reduce input costs and access economies of scale. Kmart's own-brand Anko is designed in-house and sourced directly from overseas manufacturers, cutting out intermediaries — this global sourcing strategy contributed to Kmart Group's FY2025 earnings growing 9.2% while revenue grew only 2.9%. Globalisation has also let Kmart take Anko in the opposite direction, opening Anko stores in the Philippines and securing distribution partnerships with major global retailers, turning a private label into an export product.

However, globalisation also increases exposure to global supply chains: DP World Australia's role handling around 40% of national container freight means a single disruption — such as its November 2023 cyber attack, which stranded roughly 30,000 containers — can affect operations for many Australian businesses at once. Operations managers must weigh the cost and scale advantages of global sourcing against the added supply-chain risk that comes with relying on fewer, larger, more interconnected global systems.

questions.questionHtml: A large telecommunications provider has outsourced its billing enquiries and technical support line to a provider in Cebu, reducing its labour cost for those functions by 38%. Average call-resolution time has since risen by 50%. Using the stimulus, discuss the advantages and disadvantages of outsourcing for this business.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Advantage: the cost saving achieved.
  • Disadvantage: the quality/customer-service impact.
  • Reach a conclusion.
Sample answer

The clearest advantage the telco has gained from outsourcing is cost: a 38% reduction in labour cost for billing and technical support is a substantial saving that could be redirected to other parts of the business or passed on to improve price competitiveness, and it lets the telco access an established overseas workforce without the time and cost of building that capability itself. The clear disadvantage is service quality: average call-resolution time has risen by half, suggesting the outsourced provider is not matching the efficiency the telco's own staff previously delivered, which risks customer churn and reputational damage that could ultimately cost more than the savings achieved. On balance, the outsourcing decision is only worthwhile if the telco can address the service-quality problem — through tighter service-level agreements, additional training investment or closer monitoring of the provider — since a 38% cost saving is of limited value if it drives customers to switch providers over slow support.

questions.questionHtml: Ridgeline Joinery manufactures custom staircases in Geelong. Over eighteen months its lead time has risen from three to seven weeks, its rework rate from 3% to 9%, and two competitors have begun importing pre-fabricated staircases priced 25% below its own. Recommend TWO operations strategies Ridgeline Joinery could implement to improve its performance. Justify your recommendations.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Recommendation 1: a quality-management strategy addressing the rising rework rate.
  • Recommendation 2: a strategy addressing lead time or cost competitiveness.
  • Justify each against the data given, and note a cost or risk.
Sample answer

First, Ridgeline Joinery should implement a quality management strategy, specifically quality control checkpoints at key stages of production combined with root-cause analysis of the current 9% rework rate. Since rework has risen from 3% to 9%, whatever is causing that increase is actively costing the business in wasted materials, labour and lead time — reducing rework directly attacks two of its three problems at once, because it is almost certainly a major contributor to the blow-out in lead time from three to seven weeks. Second, the business should review its scheduling and sequencing — introducing a Gantt chart or similar planning tool to identify exactly where the seven-week lead time is being lost, since without knowing which stage has slowed down, any fix is guesswork. Together, faster, more reliable production directly addresses the competitive threat from importers 25% cheaper: Ridgeline Joinery is unlikely to be able to compete purely on price against importers with lower cost bases, so restoring its lead time and quality gives it a differentiation-based case for a premium local product, rather than trying to win a price war it is not well positioned to win. The main risk is that implementing new quality checks may initially slow production further before rework falls, so the business should expect a short-term dip in output during the transition.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the strategic role of operations management?
trivia.answerHtml: Long-term planning performed by senior managers to achieve maximum output with minimum input (efficiency), adding value to the business.

trivia.questionHtml: What is cost leadership?
trivia.answerHtml: Competing by having lower prices than competitors, achieved by minimising the cost of production, e.g. Aldi.

trivia.questionHtml: What is good/service differentiation?
trivia.answerHtml: Competing on the basis of special characteristics other than price, e.g. better quality, faster delivery or clever design.

trivia.questionHtml: What are transformed resources?
trivia.answerHtml: Inputs that are converted during production — materials, information and customers.

trivia.questionHtml: What are transforming resources?
trivia.answerHtml: Inputs that carry out the transformation process — human resources and facilities.

trivia.questionHtml: What are the 4 Vs of operations?
trivia.answerHtml: Volume, variety, variation in demand and visibility.

trivia.questionHtml: What does a Gantt chart show that Critical Path Analysis doesn't?
trivia.answerHtml: A quick overview of tasks and estimated time — but not the relationship between tasks (CPA does).

trivia.questionHtml: What is the critical path in Critical Path Analysis?
trivia.answerHtml: The longest sequence of dependent tasks — the shortest possible time to complete the whole project.

trivia.questionHtml: What is FIFO?
trivia.answerHtml: First-in-first-out — the oldest stock is sold first, suited to perishable goods.

trivia.questionHtml: What is LIFO?
trivia.answerHtml: Last-in-first-out — the most recently purchased stock is sold first, suited to non-perishables like fast fashion.

trivia.questionHtml: What is JIT?
trivia.answerHtml: Just-in-time — inventory is kept at minimum levels and ordered only when needed.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the difference between quality control and quality assurance?
trivia.answerHtml: Quality control is reactive (inspecting and fixing defects); quality assurance is proactive (preventing defects before they occur).

trivia.questionHtml: What does TQM stand for?
trivia.answerHtml: Total quality management — a business-wide, continuous-improvement approach to quality.

trivia.questionHtml: What is inertia, in the context of overcoming resistance to change?
trivia.answerHtml: Psychological resistance to change, caused by fear of being replaced, fear of the new, or a preference for stability.

trivia.questionHtml: What is a process layout?
trivia.answerHtml: Arranging machines/equipment grouped by the function they perform, e.g. a restaurant kitchen.

trivia.questionHtml: What is a product layout?
trivia.answerHtml: Arranging equipment by the sequence of tasks in manufacturing, e.g. an assembly line.

trivia.questionHtml: What is a fixed position layout?
trivia.answerHtml: Employees and equipment come to the product, e.g. building a house.

trivia.questionHtml: What is a KPI?
trivia.answerHtml: A key performance indicator — used to measure the efficiency and effectiveness of a business's performance.

trivia.questionHtml: What is CAD?
trivia.answerHtml: Computer-aided design — a computerised tool for creating and visualising 3D product designs.

trivia.questionHtml: What is CAM?
trivia.answerHtml: Computer-aided manufacturing — software that uses computer technology to alter and control the manufacturing process.

trivia.questionHtml: What does supply chain management involve?
trivia.answerHtml: Integrating and managing the flow of supplies through sourcing, logistics and e-commerce to meet customer needs.

trivia.questionHtml: What is corporate social responsibility (CSR)?
trivia.answerHtml: Open and accountable business practices addressing social, environmental and economic impact, going beyond legal requirements.

trivia.questionHtml: How much did Woolworths invest in its Moorebank distribution centre, and when did it open?
trivia.answerHtml: $1.3 billion — opened 18 November 2025, its largest single investment ever.

trivia.questionHtml: How many truck movements a year is the Moorebank automation expected to remove from Australian roads?
trivia.answerHtml: An estimated 26,000 truck movements a year.

trivia.questionHtml: What happened to DP World Australia in November 2023, and what share of container freight does it handle?
trivia.answerHtml: A cyber attack (10–13 November 2023) stranded around 30,000 containers; DP World handles about 40% of Australia's container freight.

trivia.questionHtml: What did Kmart Group's FY2025 earnings and revenue growth show about its operations strategy?
trivia.answerHtml: Earnings grew 9.2% while revenue grew only 2.9% — evidence the margin was made in operations (cost leadership via Anko), not price.

trivia.questionHtml: What is Bunnings' TRIFR and how did it change in FY2025?
trivia.answerHtml: Total Recordable Injury Frequency Rate — improved from 17.0 in FY2024 to 13.7 in FY2025, though still the weakest safety result in the Wesfarmers group.

trivia.questionHtml: What did the Privacy Commissioner find about Bunnings' facial recognition technology in November 2024?
trivia.answerHtml: That its use in stores from November 2018 to November 2021 breached the Privacy Act.

trivia.questionHtml: What was REDcycle, and what happened to it in November 2022?
trivia.answerHtml: An in-store soft plastics recycling scheme run through Coles and Woolworths — it stopped processing collected plastic, leaving thousands of tonnes stockpiled rather than recycled.

trivia.questionHtml: How much stockpiled soft plastic was removed from NSW sites under EPA Clean-Up Notices, as reported in mid-2025?
trivia.answerHtml: 4,000 tonnes, removed from 15 sites across NSW.

trivia.questionHtml: Why is Qantas the standard example of operations in a tertiary industry?
trivia.answerHtml: Its product (a seat) is intangible, perishable (an unsold seat is lost forever), and produced and consumed simultaneously with high customer contact.

trivia.questionHtml: Why is Canva a useful example of operations in a quaternary/digital services business?
trivia.answerHtml: Its product has near-zero marginal cost — the operations challenge is capacity and reliability, not physical transformation of materials.

trivia.questionHtml: What is global sourcing?
trivia.answerHtml: Purchasing raw materials, components or finished goods from suppliers located overseas, usually to reduce cost or access specialist inputs.
